name: Esther Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing primary teaching, so I have lectures on child development and a lot of reading, plus one morning a week in a Year 2 classroom as a volunteer helper. I share a flat above a bakery with two girls from my course, and I work Saturdays at a second-hand bookshop. My mum's a nurse and she pays about half my rent. I've never had a week that felt this full, but I walk out of the classroom mornings feeling like I picked the right thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with teaching real children. I'd mention to friends that the tools are fine for lesson planning ideas, but children still need an adult who notices when something is wrong, and no tool will do that. And I'd say schools should still get the funding they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I don't think much changes, and that's slightly disappointing, because teachers are tired and a good tool could help with marking. I'm still worried about class sizes and pay. Teachers I volunteer with say they're leaving the job after five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. I'd keep the bookshop job, about 10 hours, and keep my volunteer morning. I'd try an AI tool for planning a lesson once or twice, to see if it's any good. And I'd join the students' union education campaign, because the pay and workload fight is not going away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. Not excited, not afraid. Just the ordinary worry about whether I'll be burned out by 25.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost on your list worries you most while you study, and what would you do if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan, honestly. Mum covers about half the rent, and the bookshop covers my food, but there's no space for a bad month. If Mum's shifts got cut, I'd go to three days at the bookshop and borrow more from the student loan company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think about the day you finish your degree. What do you picture yourself doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I picture a classroom of 28 children, me with a coffee at seven in the morning, writing the date on the board. A decent job but not a rich one. I'd like to be the teacher a kid remembers, and that doesn't need any fancy technology.

say: I'd tell friends **tools** are fine for lesson ideas, but children need an adult.
I'd say schools still need proper **funding**.
think: Nothing changes much, which is slightly disappointing, since **marking** and workload are crushing teachers.
My real worry is **burnout** and pay, not machines.
do: Keep the **bookshop** job at about 10 hours a week.
Try an AI tool to plan one **lesson** and see if it helps.
feel: **Okay**, with the ordinary worry about burnout by 25.
S0.quote: Children still need an adult who notices when something is wrong, and no tool will do that.
fieldNote: Esther's worries are about **teacher burnout** and pay, which are there with or without AI.
She is open to **trying a tool**, but only after seeing it works.
Her mum's rent help is the thin spot in her budget.

steps.text: Keep working Saturdays at the bookshop
Try an AI tool on one lesson plan
Join the students' union education campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say schools will be a big test. Planning, marking and parent emails could all be done by software, and I'd say that's fine if teachers get that time back for children. But I'd say it won't happen unless unions and governments demand it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job is half thinking work, like planning and marking, so I'd expect pressure to have bigger classes, with software doing the paperwork. That's what scares me, a school saying 'the AI saves you time, so here are ten more pupils'. I'd still have a job, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI tools properly in my second year, once I've seen what the teachers I volunteer with use. I'd write my essays myself, but I'd practise making worksheets with a tool. I'd join the teachers' union as a student member, which is cheap, and I'd ask the school about class size policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but a bit curious. If it really gave teachers their evenings back that would be great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs in your field, or the part-time work you do now, would AI touch first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bookshop would change first. They're already getting a system that does the stock orders and the website descriptions. The owner says she may keep two staff instead of four. That's my Saturday job, maybe gone by second year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change what you study, or how you study it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It wouldn't change what I study, since classroom skills stay the same. It might change how, because I'd want to learn to check what a tool produces, like spotting a worksheet with a wrong answer. A tool that makes confident mistakes in front of thirty children is a real risk.

say: I'd say software could give teachers **time back**, but only if unions demand it.
I'd say schools shouldn't use savings to enlarge **class sizes**.
think: Planning and marking are my job's **thinking half**, so I expect pressure to take more pupils.
The bookshop **Saturday job** could be cut by second year.
do: Start using AI tools for **worksheets** in second year, and check the answers.
Join the teachers' **union** as a student member.
Ask the placement school about **class size** policy.
feel: **Uneasy** but curious, because lost evenings could come back.
S1.quote: A tool that makes confident mistakes in front of thirty children is a real risk.
fieldNote: Esther sees both sides: **time saved** and a risk of bigger classes.
She plans to learn tools **only after** watching real teachers use them.
The bookshop is a concrete early example of job cuts.

steps.text: Practise making worksheets with an AI tool
Join the teachers' union as a student member
Look for a different weekend job if the bookshop cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules before anything else, because two years is far too short for schools, families or governments. I'd sign petitions and probably go to a march, which I've never done. And I'd say children's learning must not be turned over to companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm frightened. If AI does most thinking work by 2028, what does a primary teacher do? Teaching children is thinking work and care work, and I don't know if schools would still pay for the care. Parents might trust a tutor system more than me. The caring part would last, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Mum, and we'd work out the cheapest way to finish the degree. I'd get a job with more hours and move to a cheaper room. I'd also email my MP and ask the university what it's doing to prepare. If schools weren't hiring, I might switch to nursing, like Mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and a bit angry. It feels like a decision made without any of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family, and what would you do about your degree place and your loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop eating out and cut the phone contract. I'd ask Mum for a clear talk about how long she can help. I'd ask the bookshop for more shifts now, while there are still shifts. And I'd save whatever I could in case the loan became unpayable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, who or what would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on Mum, my flatmates and the union. I'd lean on my tutors to tell me honestly what schools plan. I'd go to the council too, if there was any support. I wouldn't lean on companies, because they caused it.

say: I'd say we need **rules** first, because two years is too short.
I'd sign **petitions** and go to my first march.
think: Teaching is thinking work and **care** work, and I'm unsure schools would still pay for the care.
I'd consider switching to **nursing**, like my mum.
do: Talk to **Mum** about how long she can help with rent.
Ask the bookshop for more **shifts** while shifts exist.
Email my **MP** and ask the university for its plan.
feel: **Scared** and angry that nobody asked us.
S2.quote: Teaching children is thinking work and care work, and I don't know if schools would still pay for the care.
fieldNote: Esther splits teaching into **thinking and care**, and fears only the care survives.
Nursing like her mum is her **fallback**.
Anger at **companies and governments** shapes her action.

steps.text: Have a clear money talk with Mum
Ask the bookshop for extra shifts now
Email the MP about school plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to act, but only if we start. I'd tell friends to push student unions and the local council to plan for schools now. I'd say don't wait for 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd worry, but I'd feel I could do something. By graduation in 2029 I'd be a new teacher in a school that's already changing. Children will still need classrooms, and I'd have a few years before robots. I think I'd keep my job but it would be a different job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and go to the school I volunteer in and ask if I can do more hours. I'd practise using AI planning tools, learn how to check them, and keep a savings pot of about 50 a month from the bookshop. I'd also join the teachers' union before graduating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, but calmer than with two years. A date to aim at helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in those five years compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be changing everything straight away. With five I'd finish the degree, work two years, and see how schools react. It gives me time to be good at the human part of teaching, which I think will matter more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At what point would you decide to stay on your course or change it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd decide at the end of second year, after my first long placement. If schools are cutting teacher posts or my placement school says it's not hiring, I'd think hard about nursing. If they're still short of teachers, I'd stay.

say: I'd say five years is enough **time**, if we start now.
I'd push student unions and local councils to plan for **schools** now.
think: I'd keep my **job**, but I think it would become a different job.
Robots come later, so I'd have a few **years** in the classroom first.
do: Ask the placement school for more **volunteer** hours.
Save about **50 a month** from the bookshop wage.
Practise using planning tools and **checking** what they produce.
feel: **Anxious** but calmer, because a date helps.
S3.quote: Children will still need classrooms, and I'd have a few years before robots.
fieldNote: Esther decides in **second year**, after her first long placement.
The longer runway lets her focus on the **human side** of teaching.
She keeps nursing as a **plan B**.

steps.text: Ask the placement school for more volunteer hours
Save 50 a month from bookshop wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we shouldn't waste it. I'd tell people to work out what schools should be for. And I'd say politicians should plan now, instead of panicking later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel pretty okay. By 2036 I'd be 29, with maybe six years of teaching, and the robots arrive about 2039. I'd have time to become a good teacher, maybe a head of year. The risk is that schools shrink, but it's far enough away to adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work, and pay down the loan. I'd learn the tools gradually, and keep an eye on how schools change. I'd try to move into a role that's more about pastoral care, like a learning mentor, since that's the human end of teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. Ten years feels like a normal career plan, not an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having ten years let you do that two years wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could build a career, buy a flat and maybe have a family. With two years I'd have no room for any of that. Time is what lets me plan life, not just survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's thinking of starting your degree next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to go ahead, because children will still need people who know them. I'd say learn the tools, join a union and don't count on the job staying the same. A degree in teaching gives you skills in how people learn, and that carries over.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift and politicians should plan now.
I'd ask what **schools** are really for.
think: I'd be 29 with six **teaching years** before robots arrive.
Schools might **shrink**, but ten years is far enough to adapt.
do: Finish the degree and **teach**, paying down the loan.
Learn the **tools** gradually as schools adopt them.
Aim for a **pastoral** role, like a learning mentor.
feel: **Fairly calm**, because ten years feels like a normal career plan.
S4.quote: Time is what lets me plan life, not just survive.
fieldNote: Esther moves from fear to **planning** with ten years.
She imagines a **pastoral** role as the safe human end of teaching.
Mood stays uneasy because **school funding** is already a worry.

steps.text: Teach after graduating and pay down the loan
Learn school AI tools as they arrive
Train towards a pastoral learning mentor role

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because nobody would have time to prepare and children would be caught in the middle. What would help is clear rules, schools keeping human teachers, and the university telling us honestly what it thinks is coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd like politicians to talk to young people, not just about us. We'll be living in this, and most of us don't have a lobbyist.

headlineQuote: We'll be living in this, and most of us don't have a lobbyist.
portrait: Esther is a **primary teaching** first-year, 19, in a flat above a bakery.
Her mum is a nurse and pays about half the rent, and she works at a **bookshop** on Saturdays.
She is progressive, pro-union and open to **AI tools** once others have proven them.
She splits teaching into thinking work and **care work**, and believes care will last longest.
Her moods run uneasy to anxious, and **nursing** is her fallback if schools stop hiring.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because schools and families couldn't prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **rules**, human teachers kept in schools and honest information from the university.
